title: Expert prefetch windowing: roulette scheduling notes
content:
Summary:

This doc captures notes and experimental results for a scheduling heuristic we prototyped called "roulette prefetch" intended to reduce tail jitter and hotspot blowups when serving MoE and hybrid dense+MoE models under long context workloads. The core idea: instead of deterministic per-session prefetch ordering (which amplifies hot experts and head-of-line contention), randomize prefetch target selection with a controlled bias toward higher-affinity experts and a tunable friction term that reduces repeated immediate hits.

Motivation / observed problem:
- Under long-context chat workloads (mean context length ~3k tokens, heavy session stickiness), deterministic prefetch produces recurring expert hotspots. A small set of experts gets prefetched aggressively across many sessions, generating bandwidth and KV-cache thrashing.
- Hotspot patterns lead to: increased p95/p99 token latency spikes, more GPU page faults on UVM backends, periodic PCIe/DMA bursts, and blocking serialization in expert commit paths.
- Traditional mitigation (per-session round-robin or strict affinity) either increases average latency (more misses) or simply shifts hotspots to next experts.

Roulette scheduling idea (sketch):
- Maintain per-session affinity vector A for top-K experts (K configurable). Affinity estimated from gating weights and recent dispatch history.
- For each prefetch cycle, sample M candidates from top-K with probability proportional to (A_i ^ alpha) * S_i, where alpha controls concentration and S_i is a session-specific smoothing factor that decays on repeated fetches (friction).
- Friction S_i := exp(-n_recent_hits * beta) where n_recent_hits is the count of times expert i was prefetched for this session in the last window. Beta is the friction coefficient.
- Add an entropy floor epsilon to all probabilities to guarantee exploration (prevents permanent starvation).
- Prefetch TTL: each prefetched shard has a TTL (ms) after which it becomes eligible for re-prefetch; TTL modulated by observed token reuse rate.

Implementation notes (prototype):
- Implemented in C++ prefetch planner module (prefetch_planner.cc) with parameters exposed via runtime flags: --prefetch_k --prefetch_m --prefetch_alpha --prefetch_beta --prefetch_epsilon --prefetch_ttl_ms.
- Sampling performed using reservoir sampling + alias table (for stability under high-throughput). Alias table rebuilt per-session every N cycles (N tunable) to amortize cost.
- Bookkeeping uses compact ring buffer (last 64 prefetch targets) to compute n_recent_hits cheaply.
- Metrics emitted: roulette_entropy, per-session_prefetch_skew_gini, prefetch_miss_rate, prefetch_kv_hit_ms, prefetch_bandwidth_bytes, per-expert_serialize_wait_ms.

Experiments and measurements (summary):
Testbeds:
- Models: Llama-2-13B (dense baseline), Mistral-7B, Qwen-14B, and a 32-expert MoE variant (MoE-32 derived from Mistral fork used internally).
- Hardware: DGX-A100 style nodes (8x A100 40GB) + cloud p4d equivalent runs. Both UVM and pinned CUDA modes evaluated.
- Workloads: synthetic conversational traces (zipfian expert access distribution), replay of anonymized production session traces (3M tokens), long-context stress tests (avg len 3k, tail 15k).

Key results (configs compared):
1) Deterministic affinity prefetch (baseline): prefetch_k=8, deterministic top-K order.
2) Round-robin per-session: rotate top-K by session hash.
3) Roulette (alpha=1.0, beta=0.6, epsilon=0.02, ttl=120ms, rebuild_N=16).

Observations:
- Mean token latency: all three roughly comparable (+/- 3%). Roulette incurred small 1.5% p50 increase vs deterministic in some models due to extra exploration fetches.
- Tail (p95/p99): Roulette reduced p95 by ~18% and p99 by ~25% on MoE-32 runs compared to deterministic. Round-robin reduced p95 by ~8% only.
- GPU utilization: slightly more uniform across experts with roulette; peak expert-side queue depth variance reduced by ~40%.
- KV cache hit rate: deterministic saw higher short-term hits but larger variance; roulette increased average TTL-effective hit rate over long windows because it avoided repeated eviction cycles on hot experts.
- PCIe/DMA bursts: deterministic produced frequent short bursts correlated with mass prefetch to the same expert; roulette smoothed bandwidth with lower peak bandwidth but slightly higher sustained bandwidth. Peak reduction was ~30%.
- UVM page faults: deterministic had 1.9x the page-fault rate vs roulette in worst-case long-context replay.

Model-specific notes:
- Llama-2 (dense): Roulette provided modest improvements for long-context baseline where token reuse was low — overhead not always worth it. For dense-only models prefer low alpha (0.6) and longer TTLs.
- Mistral/Qwen (dense with different kernel fits): Qwen showed higher sensitivity to increased sustained bandwidth (aliasing with its FFN tiling); need to lower M (prefetch count) for Qwen runs to avoid FFN IO saturation.
- MoE-32: Largest wins here. Hotspot mitigation directly translated to lower tail latencies and reduced expert serialization times. Optimal alpha tended to be higher (1.2–1.5) because experts have more skew in gating weights.

Profiling traces and example artifacts:
- Typical trace snippet (simplified):
  [session: s-1234] cycle 114: sample experts [3,7,12] (probs 0.48,0.3,0.22) -> prefetch shards 3,12 -> KV hit for 3 at token+6 -> friction[3]+=1 -> TTL set 120ms
  [GPU] expert 3 queue wait 12ms, expert 7 idle, DMA bandwidth 820MB/s

- Prometheus metrics we instrumented for plotting: prefetch_miss_rate{model}, prefetch_entropy, expert_queue_variance, per_bucket_p99_lat_ms. Dashboards in GHPR linked referenced above.

Open questions and gotchas:
- Friction tuning is workload-sensitive. High beta reduces repeated hits but can force exploration that costs p50. We need an adaptive beta mechanism based on observed reuse rate.
- Rebuild_N (alias table rebuild frequency) trades CPU vs sampling optimality. For high-concurrency environments tiny N recommended (4–8) but cost rises.
- Interaction with automatic batching: when prefetch windows coincide with large batch coalescing, roulette's smoothing can both help (less fanout spikes) and hurt (missed coalesces). Need to simulate joint heuristics.
- For Qwen, prefetch bytes per expert can collide with FFN tiling behavior; adding an IB (inbound) limiter per model helps.
- Edge case: sessions that are extremely short (e.g., <20 tokens) will pay fixed sampling cost. Use fast-paths to bypass roulette for short lived sessions.

Practical recommendations (for next rollout):
- Default mode: enable roulette only for models flagged as MoE or for workloads with median context >1000 tokens. Dense models default to lightweight variant (alpha=0.7, beta=0.3, ttl=250ms).
- Auto-tune: implement quick local estimator of recent per-session reuse and adjust beta and ttl adaptively. E.g., if reuse_rate > 0.6 => lower beta, else raise beta.
- Observability: add per-expert smoothed hit-rate and per-session prefetch_cost counters to help correlate tail spikes to prefetch patterns.
- Safety: guardrails to switch to deterministic when node-level memory pressure or DMA contention detected. This prevents roulette making things worse under certain infra constraints.

Next steps / TODOs:
- A/B run on dedicated cluster (week-long) against replay of production traffic (INF-1240).
- Implement adaptive beta and ttl prototype in prefetch_planner (owner: Miguel).
- Add fast-path to bypass roulette for sessions with <20 tokens / <2 prefetch cycles (owner: Priya).
- Run Qwen-specific stress with IB limiter and confirm no FFN saturation (owner: Evan).
- Draft a short runbook describing when to flip roulette on/off per model and integration with rollout policies.

Notes to self:
- Save raw traces (s3://redwood-profiling/prefetch/roulette/2024-11-06) before sweeping parameters.
- Remember to attach sampling seeds to runs for reproducibility.

End of notes.
